approachQuestion.prompt:
Rebuild the Archive. Two immutable integer arrays describe the same unknown binary tree. The first lists nodes in root-left-right order; the second lists them in left-root-right order. Every node label is unique. Return a newly allocated tree matching both arrays; empty arrays return null.

Example 1: Input: first=[8,3,6,10], second=[3,6,8,10]. Output: 8(3(-,6(-,-)),10(-,-)). Example 2: Input: first=[2,7], second=[7,2]. Output: 2(7(-,-),-). Example 3: Input: first=[], second=[]. Output: -. In the output x(left,right) uses - for missing children.

Constraints: both arrays have n elements, 0 <= n <= 200000. Labels are distinct signed 32-bit integers; the arrays contain the same set and are guaranteed to describe a valid common tree. Shape is unrestricted. Return child pointers only, without parent links. Extra indexing memory is allowed; do not change input arrays.

options.text: Build a label-to-index hash map for the second array. Use explicit construction frames with index ranges, taking the next first-array label as root. Its second-array index splits the left and right ranges; process left before right without copying slices.
options.feedback: Unique labels locate each root exactly. The second-array split determines subtree sizes, so the first-array cursor can construct the matching children.

options.text: Use the same root/range construction, but scan the active second-array range to locate its root on every call instead of indexing labels.
options.feedback: It reconstructs every valid input correctly, but repeated range scans can revisit long segments. An index map removes those scans using the permitted extra memory.

options.text: Make the middle label of each second-array range its root and recursively split around that midpoint, ignoring the first-array order.
options.feedback: This invents balance. Example 2 requires root 2, but choosing the first midpoint of [7,2] makes 7 the root.

options.text: Insert labels from the first array into a binary search tree, using numeric comparisons to place children.
options.feedback: No search-tree property is promised. first=[2,7], second=[7,2] requires 7 as a left child, while numeric insertion puts it right.

feedback.reason: Traversal boundaries and unique labels support indexed reconstruction without slicing or repeated searches.
details: Create a hash map from each second-array label to its position. Use explicit frames for inclusive/exclusive second-array ranges and output attachment slots. An empty range attaches null. Otherwise consume the next first-array label, create its node, look up its split index, and process the left range before the right range. Store range indices, not copied slices, and return the created root.

The next preorder label chooses the root, while its inorder index splits left and right ranges. Unique labels make the split unambiguous. Process ranges by indices rather than copying their slices at every recursive level.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze only the revealed indexed reconstruction for n>=1 labels and output height h. What is its tight expected-time and worst-case auxiliary-space pair? Assume hash insertion and lookup have expected constant time under uniform hashing, including amortized resizing, and the map uses O(n) space in the worst case. Count that map, cursor, and construction frames. Exclude both input arrays and all final output nodes. Node allocation is constant-time; no array slices are copied.
constraints: All legal shapes are allowed; do not assume balance. Heights count nodes, not edges.

Use expected hash costs under the uniform-hashing assumption stated in the prompt, with amortized insertion resizing; the space bound is worst case. Pointer/range arithmetic and fixed-size frame operations take constant time. Count every live construction frame and the complete map. No language recursion or input slicing is used.

feedback.reason: Index inorder positions once, then create each output node once.
details: Building the index and processing each label once takes expected O(n) time under the stated hashing model. The map uses O(n) space and frames use O(h), with h<=n.

The next first-array label is the active subtree root. Its unique second-array position partitions exactly the left and right labels. Constructing the left range first consumes precisely its labels before the right range; induction yields the unique common tree.
“Expected O(n) time, O(h) auxiliary space”: The construction stack follows height, but the label-to-index map retains n entries and must also count.
